title: Conceptual understanding
subtitle: Knowing *why* — comprehension of mathematical concepts, operations, and relations, not just the ability to perform them.

sections.sources: Grounded in NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) & the five strands of mathematical proficiency.

blocks.text: Conceptual understanding is an integrated, functional grasp of mathematical ideas — knowing not just *what* to do but *why* it works and how ideas connect.

A student with conceptual understanding sees mathematics as a web of connected ideas rather than a list of isolated rules. That connectedness is what makes knowledge durable: forgotten procedures can be reconstructed, new situations can be reasoned through, and errors get caught because something “doesn't make sense.”
What it looks like in a student

items: Can explain *why* a procedure works, not only how to run it.
Represents an idea in more than one way and links the representations.
Recognizes the same structure across different problems (a unit rate, whether it's speed, price, or slope).
Catches unreasonable answers because the concept flags them.

blocks.text: The five strands are *interdependent* — conceptual understanding grows alongside fluency and reasoning, not in a fixed sequence before them. But it's the foundation the others are most fragile without.
Instructional practices that build it — and how
These Effective Teaching Practices develop conceptual understanding most directly:

rows: Linking tables, graphs, equations, and contexts turns isolated facts into a connected web of meaning — the essence of “knowing why.”
Puts the concept before the procedure, so skills rest on ideas students actually understand rather than steps they memorized.
“Why does that work?” forces the underlying idea into the open and presses students to make it explicit.
Comparing and connecting classmates' approaches exposes the big idea sitting beneath all of them.

blocks.text: In the toolbelt, this shows up in [Number Talks](/math/approach/number-talks), [Connecting Representations](/math/approach/connecting-representations), and [Same But Different / WODB](/math/approach/same-but-different) — all of which keep the “why” at the center.

A student who can execute a procedure flawlessly but can't say why it works, or when to use it, does *not* yet have conceptual understanding — and that fluency is likely to fade. Speed and accuracy alone are not evidence of this strand.
“Why does that work?” — and its cousin, “show me another way.” If a student can only answer “because that's the rule,” the understanding isn't there yet.
